Kotlin Multiplatform, from the compiler up · Puzzle 5 · 6 of 10

Two ways to free memory

Your shared Kotlin runs inside an iOS app. Kotlin's objects are freed one way, Swift's another. Here's what happens where they hold on to each other.

Builds on: open one to see the idea this puzzle uses.

  • Puzzle 2: A promise and its keepers

    An expect declaration in common code is a promise; every platform source set keeps it with an actual declaration. The compiler checks that every target has one. For anything bigger, an interface implemented per platform does the same job and is easier to test.

Starting from zero? The blocks under this puzzle are 3 puzzles: 0 → 1 → 2. Know them already? Start here.

The problem

In module 1, your Kotlin compiled to native code inside an iOS app. On Android, the garbage collector frees your objects. Swift frees its objects with ARC, the moment nothing refers to them (the iOS course, puzzle 4). Now a Swift screen holds your Kotlin view model, and the view model keeps a callback that points back at the screen. Who frees what, and when?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

Kotlin/Native keeps its objects in a shared heap: one pool of objects any thread can use, like on the JVM. From time to time a tracing GC runs: it starts from the roots, such as local and global variables, follows every reference, and frees everything it couldn't reach. That's the garbage collector you know from Android.

Swift objects are freed by ARC: each counts its strong references and is freed when the count hits zero.

Where the two meet, each side follows its own rules:

  • A Kotlin object that Swift holds stays alive while Swift holds it: to the GC, Swift's hold counts as a root.
  • A Swift object that Kotlin holds isn't freed the moment Kotlin lets go. It's freed at the next GC, when the collector finds Kotlin no longer reaches it. So Swift's deinit can run later than a Swift developer expects.
  • A cycle that runs through both sides, Kotlin to Swift and back, can leak. Each side holds the other, and neither tool sees the whole loop.

The fix is the one from the iOS course: make one link weak. Usually the Swift side holds the Kotlin object normally and the callback refers back to the Swift object weakly: in Swift, capture it with [weak self] in the closure you hand to Kotlin.

The analogy

Two cities that clean their streets differently: one sends a sweeper round every few days (the GC), the other picks up each item the moment its owner lets go (ARC). An item two neighbours from different cities each keep "for the other one" is never picked up by either.

Check yourself

Kotlin holds a Swift object, then lets go. When does Swift's deinit run?

Right. Release follows Kotlin's GC, not the moment of letting go.

Not quite. It's freed, only later: at the next garbage collection.

Not quite. Kotlin's hold is released by the collector, so the Swift object waits for the next GC.

Why can a cycle through both Kotlin and Swift leak?

Right. Two tools, each seeing half the loop.

Not quite. ARC counts fine; the trouble is the loop that runs through both.

Not quite. The GC runs on iOS too; it just can't see past Swift's hold, which counts as a root.

What's the difference between a tracing GC and ARC?

Right. Search in passes vs count as you go.

Not quite. That's the two swapped.

Not quite. Counting is ARC's way; a tracing GC follows references from the roots.

Sources

  • Kotlin docs: Kotlin/Native memory management ("Objects are stored in a shared heap and can be accessed from any thread. Tracing garbage collection is performed periodically to collect objects that are not reachable from the 'roots', like local and global variables.")
  • Kotlin docs: Integration with Swift/Objective-C ARC ("An object is reclaimed only during the garbage collection. This applies to Swift/Objective-C objects that cross interop boundaries into Kotlin/Native"; "To avoid retain cycles, use weak or unowned references")

What you now know

Kotlin/Native keeps objects in a shared heap and frees them with a tracing GC, like the JVM. Swift frees with ARC. A Swift object held by Kotlin is only freed at a GC, not the moment it's let go; and a cycle that runs through both sides can leak. Break it with a weak reference on the Swift side.
